content: The analysis included 26 studies, of which 18 involved surgical interventions and 8 did not. All studies were observational in nature, introducing a significant risk of selection bias. The selection of patients for surgery may have been influenced by their prognostic factors, either favoring those with better outcomes or the opposite. Additionally, the duration of treatment varied considerably between surgical and non-surgical patients, suggesting that differences in background medical regimens could also impact outcomes. These potential confounders were accounted for in the adjusted analysis. Inconsistencies were noted, as indicated by the I-squared statistic. The odds ratio (OR) for treatment success increased when individuals lost to follow-up were included in the analysis. However, no indirectness was expected, as all patients were undergoing treatment for multidrug-resistant (MDR) or extensively drug-resistant (XDR) tuberculosis (TB). The outcomes assessed—success, treatment failure, relapse, and death—were deemed critical by the Guideline Development Group. Loss to follow-up, while not a specified outcome, was relevant to the analysis. The precision of the effect estimates was evaluated using 95% confidence intervals. Pooled proportions for treatment success varied across studies, with values such as 79% (71–88%), 77% (6–85%), 69% (60–78%), 64% (54–73%), 62% (54–71%), and 51% (40–62%). Adjusted effect estimates were derived using one-to-one propensity score matching between surgical and non-surgical patients. The focus of the analysis was on standardized shorter regimens versus longer regimens for treating MDR-TB. Shorter regimens, lasting up to 12 months, were compared to longer regimens, which typically lasted 18 months or more. Early results from observational studies in Bangladesh, Cameroon, and Niger demonstrated higher treatment success rates with shorter regimens among patients meeting specific inclusion criteria. However, due to limited experience with these regimens, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended their use only within operational research settings and under close monitoring for safety and effectiveness. Shorter regimens have been associated with relapse-free cure rates exceeding 85% in selected patients, compared to longer regimens. However, data on their performance in the presence of additional drug resistance remain scarce. Patients previously treated with second-line drugs or those with known resistance to key drugs in the regimen were excluded from these studies. In regions with more extensive resistance patterns, such as Eastern Europe and Central Asia, the effectiveness of shorter regimens may be reduced. The use of shorter regimens has been linked to fewer adverse events, even when these were systematically collected in operational research settings. Gatifloxacin, a key component of shorter regimens, was previously associated with dysglycemia in elderly patients treated for non-TB conditions. However, subsequent studies showed no increased risk of dysglycemia when gatifloxacin was used in four-month TB regimens. The benefits of gatifloxacin are considered to outweigh the risks in the treatment of MDR-TB. Additionally, shorter regimens exclude several drugs commonly associated with severe adverse events, such as cycloserine, para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), and linezolid. The overall certainty of evidence for the effects of shorter regimens is very low, as all data were derived from observational studies. Randomized controlled trial data are not expected until after 2017. Despite this, the balance of desirable and undesirable effects likely favors the intervention, as shorter regimens have demonstrated higher treatment success rates and lower adverse event rates compared to longer regimens. The cost-effectiveness of shorter regimens is expected to be favorable, as both drug and program costs are unlikely to exceed those of longer regimens. The intervention has been successfully implemented in various settings in Africa and Asia, with support from technical agencies and national programs. However, challenges remain, such as the limited availability of quality-assured gatifloxacin and clofazimine, which are essential components of shorter regimens. WHO recommends that shorter regimens should not be used in patients previously treated with second-line drugs for more than one month or those with known resistance to key drugs in the regimen. Patients should be tested for resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents before starting treatment. In the absence of reliable testing, patients with a low likelihood of infection with resistant strains may still be eligible for shorter regimens. Special considerations apply to certain populations. People living with HIV should be treated with the same shorter regimens as HIV-negative individuals. Children, although generally excluded from studies, are not expected to respond differently to shorter regimens and should be considered for the same treatment. Pregnant women were excluded from studies due to the contraindication of key drugs in the regimen, such as injectable agents and ethionamide. Extrapulmonary TB was not directly studied, and no recommendation can be made for the use of shorter regimens in these cases. To replicate the high cure rates observed in studies, careful patient selection and effective support to ensure full adherence to treatment are essential. Resistance testing for fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents should be conducted before initiating shorter regimens.
